statements.quote: A single text prompt, and a diffusion model produced this image in seconds.
This one was created with the prompt “Astronaut Riding a Horse” (\cite[Image: Stable Diffusion 3.5]{diffusion_astronaut_img})
Most of AI's image generators used to be delicate.
GANs collapsed, VAEs blurred, and training them was an art.

Then in 2020, a paper called **DDPM** (\cite[Ho et al., 2020]{ho2020ddpm}) turned a 2015 idea from Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues (\cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015]{sohl2015deep}) into a practical recipe: learn to reverse a fixed noising process.
A parallel line, score-based generation (\cite[Song & Ermon, 2019]{song2019score}), was converging on the same object from the other side.
Within two years, Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 2, Imagen, and Midjourney had made **diffusion** the dominant way to generate images.
By 2024 it had spread to video (Sora, Veo), audio, music, and even 3D protein structures.
The idea is almost paradoxical: instead of generating an image in one forward pass, **destroy an image with noise step by step, then learn to undo the destruction, one tiny step at a time**.
It is a different paradigm from the autoregressive next-token prediction that drives LLMs, even though both produce staggering results.
The idea is older than the image generators that made it famous.

\cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015)]{sohl2015deep} introduced diffusion probabilistic models in 2015 as a way to learn a generative distribution by reversing a thermodynamic relaxation: gradually destroy structure with a fixed Markov chain, then train a network to run that chain backward (\cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015]{sohl2015deep}).
The method worked on small datasets but was expensive and did not beat the generative models of the day.
Its revival waited for a better training objective and a better architecture.
Not every system in that wave was a diffusion model.

**DALL·E** (2021) was a 12-billion-parameter autoregressive Transformer over discrete image tokens, a direct application of the language-model recipe to pixels; **DALL·E 2** then switched to diffusion conditioned on CLIP *text* embeddings, using a prior to map them into image-embedding space, and the rest of the field followed (\cite[Ramesh et al., 2022]{ramesh2022dalle2}); the 2021 DALL·E paper describes the earlier autoregressive system (\cite[Ramesh et al., 2021]{ramesh2021dalle}).
The brief autoregressive detour is a useful reminder that “predict the next token” is architecture-agnostic: the token can be a word, an image patch, or an audio frame.

statements.quote: If you would rather read the foundational papers, the trio that started it all is Sohl-Dickstein's 2015 thermodynamic framing (\cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015]{sohl2015deep}), Song & Ermon's score-based 2019 paper (\cite[Song & Ermon, 2019]{song2019score}), and Ho's DDPM in 2020 (\cite[Ho et al., 2020]{ho2020ddpm}).
statements.section: Try it yourself

blocks.quote: A single text prompt, and a diffusion model produced this image in seconds. This one was created with the prompt “Astronaut Riding a Horse” (\cite[Image: Stable Diffusion 3.5]{diffusion_astronaut_img})

Most of AI's image generators used to be delicate. GANs collapsed, VAEs blurred, and training them was an art. Then in 2020, a paper called **DDPM** (\cite[Ho et al., 2020]{ho2020ddpm}) turned a 2015 idea from Jascha Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues (\cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015]{sohl2015deep}) into a practical recipe: learn to reverse a fixed noising process. A parallel line, score-based generation (\cite[Song & Ermon, 2019]{song2019score}), was converging on the same object from the other side. Within two years, Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 2, Imagen, and Midjourney had made **diffusion** the dominant way to generate images. By 2024 it had spread to video (Sora, Veo), audio, music, and even 3D protein structures.

The idea is almost paradoxical: instead of generating an image in one forward pass, **destroy an image with noise step by step, then learn to undo the destruction, one tiny step at a time**. It is a different paradigm from the autoregressive next-token prediction that drives LLMs, even though both produce staggering results.

The idea is older than the image generators that made it famous. \cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015)]{sohl2015deep} introduced diffusion probabilistic models in 2015 as a way to learn a generative distribution by reversing a thermodynamic relaxation: gradually destroy structure with a fixed Markov chain, then train a network to run that chain backward (\cite[Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015]{sohl2015deep}). The method worked on small datasets but was expensive and did not beat the generative models of the day. Its revival waited for a better training objective and a better architecture.

Not every system in that wave was a diffusion model. **DALL·E** (2021) was a 12-billion-parameter autoregressive Transformer over discrete image tokens, a direct application of the language-model recipe to pixels; **DALL·E 2** then switched to diffusion conditioned on CLIP *text* embeddings, using a prior to map them into image-embedding space, and the rest of the field followed (\cite[Ramesh et al., 2022]{ramesh2022dalle2}); the 2021 DALL·E paper describes the earlier autoregressive system (\cite[Ramesh et al., 2021]{ramesh2021dalle}). The brief autoregressive detour is a useful reminder that “predict the next token” is architecture-agnostic: the token can be a word, an image patch, or an audio frame.
The diffusion process
blocks.section: The diffusion process

blocks.quote: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo
blocks.section: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo

blocks.quote: Imagine dropping a clear photograph into a glass of water and slowly stirring in drops of black ink. After each drop the picture becomes a little less recognizable. After enough drops, all you see is uniform grey.
blocks.section: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo

blocks.quote: Now imagine the reverse: starting with grey water, learn to *remove* exactly the right amount of ink, drop by drop, until a coherent photograph reappears. If you can learn that reverse process well enough, you can start from *any* grey water and turn it into a fresh, novel photograph.
blocks.section: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo

blocks.quote: That is what a diffusion model does. The forward process (ink going in) is a hand-designed procedure with no learned parameters. The reverse process (ink coming out) is what a neural network has to learn.
blocks.section: The central trick: destroy, then learn to undo

blocks.quote: The forward process: a controlled demolition
blocks.section: The forward process: a controlled demolition

blocks.quote: The slider below shows the forward process happening to a real image. Drag it to watch the picture dissolve into noise.
blocks.section: The forward process: a controlled demolition

blocks.quote: The reverse process: the part that learns
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: The reverse process starts from pure noise and runs backward. At each step, the network looks at the current noisy image and asks: *what noise should I subtract to make this slightly more recognizable?* A thousand such tiny denoising steps, and out pops a clean image.
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: DDPM's contribution was to make the reverse chain trainable by a simple surrogate. Instead of predicting the full reverse distribution, the network predicts the noise that was added, and training minimizes squared error to it — a reweighted variational bound, and the reweighting is what made sample quality jump (\cite[Ho et al., 2020]{ho2020ddpm}). \cite[Nichol & Dhariwal (2021)]{nichol2021improved} then replaced the linear noise schedule with a cosine one and learned the reverse variances, improving both log-likelihood and sample quality (\cite[Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021]{nichol2021improved}); \cite[Dhariwal & Nichol (2021)]{dhariwal2021diffusion} added classifier guidance and showed diffusion could beat GANs on image synthesis (\cite[Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021]{dhariwal2021diffusion}).
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: 3. Ask the network to predict *what that noise was*.
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: 4. Train by mean-squared error between the predicted and the true noise.
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: For the vanilla DDPM objective — and for DDIM, which is a *sampler* for a DDPM-trained model rather than a separate training recipe — that is it: no discriminator, no generator, no min-max game (\cite[Song et al., 2020]{song2020ddim}). Just MSE between predicted and true noise. This stability is one of the big reasons diffusion displaced GANs so quickly. (One caveat: the 1-step “Turbo” models like SDXL-Turbo were *not* trained with pure MSE, they use **adversarial diffusion distillation**, an explicit GAN-style loss, to compress 50 denoising steps into 1.)
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: The slider below steps through the **reverse** process on the same image. Drag it from right to left to watch an image emerge from chaos. In a real diffusion model this would take a thousand tiny denoising steps; here we collapse them into a handful of frames.
blocks.section: The reverse process: the part that learns

blocks.quote: Why does this work?
blocks.section: Why does this work?

blocks.quote: You might ask: how can *removing noise* ever create a picture? The trick is this, **a denoiser that can spot noise must also have learned what “no noise” looks like**. It has implicitly learned the shape of the data distribution. So if you start from pure noise and repeatedly denoise, you trace a path through that distribution, and end up with a brand new sample.
blocks.section: Why does this work?

blocks.quote: That is the deep “why” of diffusion in one sentence. Two ways to make it more concrete:
blocks.section: Why does this work?

blocks.quote: Either view explains why “denoising” and “generation” are two sides of the same coin.
blocks.section: Why does this work?

blocks.quote: The two lineages — denoising diffusion and score matching — were unified in 2021. \cite[Song et al. (2021)]{song2021sde} showed that both are discretizations of a stochastic differential equation: a forward SDE adds noise, and a reverse-time SDE, driven by the score, removes it (\cite[Song et al., 2021]{song2021sde}). That view made the sampler a design choice rather than a consequence of the training chain. \cite[Song et al. (2020)]{song2020ddim} had already shown the point concretely: a non-Markovian, deterministic reverse process can sample a DDPM model in far fewer steps with little loss in quality (\cite[Song et al., 2020]{song2020ddim}).
blocks.section: Why does this work?

blocks.quote: Conditioning and the model
blocks.section: Conditioning and the model

blocks.quote: Telling the model what to draw
blocks.section: Telling the model what to draw

blocks.quote: To make a model draw *what you want*, you have to feed it some signal. For text-to-image, that signal is a text prompt, first encoded into a sequence of token vectors by a separate text encoder (typically CLIP or T5).
blocks.section: Telling the model what to draw

blocks.quote: Guidance began with a classifier. \cite[Dhariwal & Nichol (2021)]{dhariwal2021diffusion} showed that a pretrained image classifier's gradient could steer each denoising step toward a chosen class, a trick called classifier guidance that improved sample quality at the cost of an extra network (\cite[Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021]{dhariwal2021diffusion}). \cite[Ho & Salimans (2022)]{ho2022cfg} removed the classifier: train one denoiser with the condition randomly dropped, then extrapolate away from its unconditional prediction (\cite[Ho & Salimans, 2022]{ho2022cfg}). That is the version Stable Diffusion uses, because it needs no classifier and works with free-form text.
blocks.section: Telling the model what to draw

blocks.quote: The trick that made text-to-image *actually work* is **classifier-free guidance** (\cite[Ho & Salimans, 2022]{ho2022cfg}). At training time, the network is shown the text prompt 90% of the time and *nothing* 10% of the time, learning both a conditional and an unconditional denoiser in one model. At inference, you amplify the gap between them:
blocks.section: Telling the model what to draw

blocks.quote: From text to image: the whole pipeline
blocks.section: From text to image: the whole pipeline

blocks.quote: The CFG trick above answers “how do you amplify the prompt”. But three questions remain: **where do the (image, prompt) training pairs come from?**, **how does the text encoder turn words into something the U-Net can read?**, and **how does the U-Net actually use those numbers?** This section walks through the full pipeline end-to-end.
blocks.section: From text to image: the whole pipeline

blocks.quote: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed
blocks.section: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed

blocks.quote: You do **not** need to sit down and label 100,000 images. The training set for Stable Diffusion is **LAION-5B**, a publicly released scrape of about 5 billion (image, alt-text) pairs from the web. The “label” of every image is whatever its surrounding HTML already said, the alt attribute, the caption, the page title.
blocks.section: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed

blocks.quote: What the model actually learns from this data is **not a database of specific images**. It learns an *internal representation of the world*: what astronauts look like, what horses look like, what “riding” looks like, what “in space” looks like, each concept distilled from many thousands of images seen during training. When you prompt for “an astronaut riding a horse”, there is almost certainly no training image of exactly that scene. The model composes a new image by combining its learned concepts: astronaut-shape here, horse-shape there, riding-pose between them. The output is **synthesized**, not retrieved.
blocks.section: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed

blocks.quote: This is also why diffusion models sometimes hallucinate or get details wrong: the “labels” are noisy, scraped web text, not clean annotations, and the concepts are statistical, not encyclopedic.
blocks.section: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed

blocks.quote: (One consequence worth knowing: as more AI-generated images flood the web, future models trained on the same web will be trained on their own predecessors' outputs. This recursive phenomenon is called **model collapse**, and it is a real research concern.)
blocks.section: 1. Training data, no manual labels needed

blocks.quote: 2. Text becomes numbers, the text encoder and embeddings
blocks.section: 2. Text becomes numbers, the text encoder and embeddings

blocks.quote: The diffusion U-Net cannot read English. Before it ever sees your prompt, a separate **text encoder** turns the prompt into a sequence of vectors. For Stable Diffusion 1.5, that encoder is CLIP's text tower; SD 3 combines CLIP-L, CLIP-G and T5-XXL, and FLUX combines CLIP-L with T5-XXL. Both are **Transformer encoders**, the same architecture family as the LLMs in the other chapters.
blocks.section: 2. Text becomes numbers, the text encoder and embeddings

blocks.quote: The text encoder does two things, in order, tokenization and embedding. Both are covered in detail elsewhere on this site (see the **Tokenization** and **Embeddings** chapters); the small viz above is just a quick reminder of what comes out of the other end of that pipeline. The crucial property for our purposes is that each token ends up as a vector (768 numbers for CLIP, 4096 for T5-XXL), and **similar concepts end up close together** in that vector space: “astronaut” and “space suit” have nearby vectors, “horse” and “pony” have nearby vectors, “astronaut riding a horse” is far from “still life with fruit”.
blocks.section: 2. Text becomes numbers, the text encoder and embeddings

blocks.quote: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: Now the diffusion U-Net has two inputs at every denoising step:
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: The U-Net applies **cross-attention** at each layer. The picture to keep in your head: **at every step, the model paints the image by asking each word in your prompt, “which part of the picture is yours?”** The word *“astronaut”* claims the upper-center region. The word *“horse”* claims the lower region. The word *“riding”* claims the bit in between. Function words like *“a”*, *“of”* barely claim anything.
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: Below: click any *content* word in the prompt and watch a colored region light up over the part of the astronaut image that word would “claim” during generation. The regions are simplified, a real diffusion model has hundreds of tiny patches, but the principle is the same: each word in your prompt controls its own piece of the picture.
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: This is the mechanism behind every text-to-image model. Different words control different regions. By the end of denoising, each pixel of the image has been “asked” which word it should look like, and the text embedding has answered. **If you swap one word in the prompt, the embedding moves, the attention shifts, and the generated image changes in just that region.** The full Stable Diffusion pipeline looks like this end-to-end:
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: The Stable Diffusion pipeline: a text encoder turns your prompt into vectors, the U-Net denoises a latent tensor conditioned on those vectors (via cross-attention), and a frozen VAE decoder turns the clean latent back into pixels. \cite[Image: Stable Diffusion architecture]{diffusion_architecture_img}
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: So the answer to “do I need to label 100k images?” is: **no** for pretraining (the labels already exist on the web). The yes cases are *fine-tuning*, if you want the model to draw a specific style or subject, you can fine-tune with **LoRA** (\cite[Hu et al., 2021]{hu2021lora}) on as few as a few dozen images, or steer outputs with **ControlNet** (\cite[Zhang et al., 2023]{zhang2023controlnet}) using edge maps, depth maps, or pose skeletons.
blocks.section: 3. Cross-attention, how the U-Net reads the text

blocks.quote: What's the network?
blocks.section: What's the network?

blocks.quote: The denoiser's shape is borrowed from medical imaging. The **U-Net** was introduced by \cite[Ronneberger et al. (2015)]{ronneberger2015unet} for biomedical segmentation, where a contracting path captures context and a symmetric expanding path restores fine detail, with skip connections passing high-resolution features across (\cite[Ronneberger et al., 2015]{ronneberger2015unet}). Diffusion models adopted it because denoising is also a dense, image-to-image prediction: every latent cell needs an output, and coarse structure and fine texture must be combined. \cite[Nichol & Dhariwal (2021)]{nichol2021improved} and \cite[Dhariwal & Nichol (2021)]{dhariwal2021diffusion} then tuned this backbone with residual blocks, attention and time embeddings.
blocks.section: What's the network?

blocks.quote: It is **not** a stack of dense layers. The denoiser is a **U-Net** built from:
blocks.section: What's the network?

blocks.quote: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: Doing all this in raw pixel space at $512 \times 512$ resolution is brutally expensive. Each image is roughly 786,000 numbers, and the network must process hundreds of millions of them per step.
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: Compressing before generating was not new. Autoencoders had long learned compact codes (\cite[Kingma & Welling, 2014]{kingma2014vae}), and VQGAN showed that a discrete autoencoder plus a powerful prior could synthesise high-resolution images (\cite[Esser et al., 2021]{esser2021taming}). \cite[Rombach et al. (2022)]{rombach2022ldm} made the decisive move for diffusion: train the autoencoder first, freeze it, and run the diffusion process entirely in its latent space (\cite[Rombach et al., 2022]{rombach2022ldm}). The result was not just cheaper — it let the same denoiser scale to larger images by changing the decoder, not the diffusion model.
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: The breakthrough of **Latent Diffusion Models** (\cite[Rombach et al., 2022]{rombach2022ldm}), the technology behind Stable Diffusion, was to *first* compress the image into a much smaller latent representation using a pretrained autoencoder, *then* do all the diffusion work in that compressed space, *then* decode the result back to pixels. The U-Net never sees a pixel; it only sees a $64 \times 64$ latent map. This makes training and inference roughly 64× cheaper.
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: The text prompt goes through CLIP, the latent goes through the U-Net, and at the end a frozen VAE decoder turns the clean latent back into an image. The VAE is never trained alongside the diffusion model, it was learned earlier as an ordinary autoencoder and frozen in place.
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: Below, the famous DDIM denoising sequence for a real Stable Diffusion run shows the same idea in action. Read it from top-left to bottom-right: the network starts from pure noise and gradually reveals a coherent image of a European-style castle in Japan, adding detail with each step.
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: Each frame is one denoising step of a Stable Diffusion 1.5 model using DDIM sampling. Early steps establish rough shapes and color fields; later steps refine texture and fine detail. \cite[Image: DDIM denoising steps]{diffusion_ddim_img}
blocks.section: Stable Diffusion: doing it in a compressed space

blocks.quote: Beyond images
blocks.section: Beyond images

blocks.quote: The same recipe works anywhere you can define a “noising” process and a network that can reverse it:
blocks.section: Beyond images

blocks.quote: The general principle is almost embarrassingly simple: **if you can blur it, you can unblur it; and if you can unblur it, you can generate it from scratch.**
blocks.section: Beyond images

blocks.quote: Where the field is now
blocks.section: Where the field is now

blocks.quote: By 2025, many new systems use **flow matching** (\cite[Lipman et al., 2023]{lipman2023flow}) or its rectified-flow variant, in which the path between data and noise is trained to be straighter than the curved diffusion path. FLUX and Stable Diffusion 3 use rectified flow; DDPM/DDIM-style samplers remain widespread in older and distilled models.
blocks.section: Where the field is now

blocks.quote: The dominant backbone is no longer the U-Net but the **Diffusion Transformer (DiT)** (\cite[Peebles & Xie, 2023]{peebles2023dit}), a vanilla Vision Transformer scaled up. Sora, FLUX, and Stable Diffusion 3 all use DiT-style backbones. The pattern is familiar: U-Net worked, then Transformers worked better once they were big enough.
blocks.section: Where the field is now

blocks.quote: Practical models have also become fast. Modern systems generate images in **1–8 network evaluations** through clever solvers (DPM-Solver, EDM) and adversarial distillation (SDXL-Turbo, LCM). Diffusion is no longer slow.
blocks.section: Where the field is now

blocks.quote: In five years, the technique went from “diffusion as a curiosity” to “diffusion as the universal generative recipe” for images, video, audio, and molecules.
blocks.section: Where the field is now

blocks.quote: Diffusion for text: language models that denoise
blocks.section: Diffusion for text: language models that denoise

blocks.quote: Text adds a wrinkle: tokens are discrete, so you cannot gradually add Gaussian noise to them. The dominant fix is an **absorbing-state** process. Each token is independently replaced by a special `[MASK]` symbol with probability $\beta_t$ per step, and once masked it stays masked:
blocks.section: Diffusion for text: language models that denoise

blocks.quote: Training is then a weighted masked-token cross-entropy over randomly sampled masking rates — BERT's fill-in-the-blank loss, rearranged into a generative process (\cite[Austin et al., 2021]{austin2021d3pm}). Sampling starts from a fully masked sequence, predicts every masked position in parallel, and commits the confident ones; easy tokens lock in first and hard content words last. This is a **diffusion language model** (dLLM), and it replaces left-to-right decoding with a handful of bidirectional denoising passes.
blocks.section: Diffusion for text: language models that denoise

blocks.quote: The promise is throughput: one forward pass can commit many tokens, and the step count is an explicit quality-versus-speed dial. **LLaDA** (2025), an 8B masked-diffusion model trained from scratch, reported instruction following competitive with Llama 3 8B — the first evidence that the recipe holds at open-model scale (\cite[Nie et al., 2025]{nie2025llada}); Inception Labs' Mercury and Google DeepMind's Gemini Diffusion followed. The cost is that bidirectional attention is incompatible with the standard KV cache, so each step recomputes over the whole sequence, and quality parity with autoregressive models at the frontier is still unresolved. The architectural comparison is in [Beyond Transformers](alternative_architectures.php).
